claims.text: **The multiplication claim:** a deterministic algorithm for one fixed multitape Turing machine, running in O(n(lg n)^(1−κ)) with κ = 2⁻¹⁸², for every input length.
An Ω(n log n) lower bound has been proved only for *on-line* machines and restricted circuit models.
**Is it Lean-verified?** No. The integer-multiplication family (109) has no Lean documentation page and is not in `formalization.yaml` [^9,15].
**Release-wide Lean coverage:** 162 papers and 185 declarations out of 722 manuscripts, with the manifest marked "unchecked" [^9].
It is not yet a body of accepted theorems, and the advisory group whose guidance shaped it explicitly declined to endorse the process [^1,33].
OpenAI's README says "the current catalogue contains 722 manuscripts organized into 372 families".
The same README says the model "was posed approximately 4,000 problems", and that results were kept only if they met "an appropriate level of significance" [^1].
On average each result used "three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute" with the unreleased model [^1].
{term: Production window, def: "Manuscript folders dated 10 September to 6 October 2026 [^16]"}
In the part of `CONTENTS.md` that could be read (families 001–056), one family, 034 on log abundance, holds 14 manuscripts, and families 014 and 032 hold 8 each [^16].
Family numbers also skip: no family 045, 061 or 070 appears in `overview.tex` [^15].
ARA checked four sections against `overview.tex` (number theory 31, algebraic and complex geometry 36, analysis 16, convex geometry 15).
No per-problem outcome table and no failure count are published [^1,38].
Its abstract describes "a deterministic algorithm that multiplies two n-bit integers in O(n(lg n)^(1−κ)) worst-case time, with κ = 2⁻¹⁸²" [^2].
The author line reads simply "OpenAI", dated 23 September 2026 [^2].
{term: Model, def: "Fixed multitape Turing machine; 'No random-access simulation is used' [^3]"}
{term: Corollaries, def: "k×k bit-matrix transposition, exact division and integer square root at the same bound [^7]"}
{term: Structure, def: "Introduction plus ten section files and an appendix [^2]"}
Its history section cites Schönhage's 1980 linear-time multiplication on storage-modification machines, and a sub-logarithmic saving on a unit-cost RAM with excluded preprocessing.
Schönhage's pointer machines do multiply in O(n) [^26], and on a log-RAM the original Schönhage–Strassen algorithm already runs in O(n) word operations [^27].
Address-field interchange and Fourier butterfly layers are performed by fixed linear networks that "form XOR combinations of intermediate data, even though its final effect is a permutation" [^4].
Each unit of rank costs one recursive call on a V/W volume, so the recursion is F_k ≤ (s/W)F_{k−1} + O(1) [^5].
The introduction says the strict inequality s < Wm "is the source of the power saving" [^3].
The assembly section takes the smallest margin in its cost table, 2⁻¹⁸¹, and keeps half: "Thus min_i g_i = 2⁻¹⁸¹ = 2κ" [^6].
Hacker News commenter keeganryan noted it "would traditionally be hidden as n lg n ^ (1 - eps) for some eps > 0" [^29].
The paper concedes that "the constants and thresholds in the construction are extremely large" [^3].
For comparison, Harvey and van der Hoeven's O(n log n) algorithm has a threshold of 2^(1729¹²) bits [^19].
Production libraries such as GMP still use Toom variants and a Fermat-style Schönhage–Strassen FFT [^28].
Harvey himself wrote in 2019 that he "would be very surprised if the conjecture turned out to be wrong" [^20].
Its truth turns on one finite gadget with a relative rank deficit of about 10⁻¹¹ [^5].
Harvey and van der Hoeven settled the upper half in *Annals of Mathematics* in 2021: O(n log n) bit operations on a multitape Turing machine [^18].
In 2025 Harvey and van der Hoeven proved that "if matrix transposition is as hard as expected, then integer multiplication is also as hard as expected" [^24].
Their paper also observes that "virtually no non-trivial (i.e. superlinear) lower bounds are known for basic computational tasks such as transposition" [^24].
OpenAI's manuscript uses their reduction in the forward direction to claim O(k²(lg k)^(1−κ)) transposition [^7].
Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen showed in 2019 that, if a central network-coding conjecture holds, "any constant degree boolean circuit for multiplication must have size Ω(n lg n)" [^23].
Search-engine summaries have claimed the OpenAI result would refute that conjecture.
The manuscript never states whether its machine is oblivious, and never mentions network coding [^4].
The rank budget comes from Frankl–Wilson-type set systems and index-coding ideas [^5].
The deficit that buys the whole saving is tiny, about 1.5 × 10⁻¹¹ in relative terms, so a single sign or rank error anywhere erases it [^5].
No Lean formalization exists for family 109. `lean/docs/109.md` returns 404, and no entry in `formalization.yaml` covers integer multiplication [^9,15].
The closest formal artifact concerns exact-DFT *linear circuits over ℂ* along a subsequence of lengths, which is a different model and a weaker statement [^9].
"An explicit power saving for the exact discrete Fourier transform", dated 25 September, claims O(n(log n)^(1−10⁻¹³)) operations in an algebraic model with "unit-cost logarithmic-size indexing" [^8].
That is a RAM-like setting, unlike the multiplication paper's tape model, and the main paper says the DFT result is not a consequence of it [^8,3].
The Hacker News thread had 91 points and 62 comments when fetched on 7 October [^29].
Commenters joked about the exponent ("2^-182 is very funny but it's bigger than 0") and asked "Is there an associated machine-checked proof of this?" [^29].
An X post by @AcerFur on 6 October read: "oh yeah btw guys we can do integer multiplication faster than n log n lol" [^43].
No complexity-theory blog had analysed the paper by 7 October, and Gil Kalai's same-day post addressed the release only in general [^35].
OpenAI's README says "Many, but not all, of the manuscripts have been formalized" and "Some of the unformalized results could have issues" [^1].
It lists 162 source papers and 185 main-result declarations, on toolchain `leanprover/lean4:v4.34.1` [^9,14].

The secondary figure that circulated, "235 of the 372 result families link to a Lean formalization page, and 162 papers have a fully formalized main result", comes from Tech Insider relaying a FourWeekMBA count [^37].
Kingy.ai's careful version calls its count "not a measured proof-pass percentage" [^38].
ARA's own reading of families 001–055 in `CONTENTS.md` found Lean links on 22 of 55 (40%), well below the 63% that 235/372 implies [^16].
An HN commenter's "about 80% of what I checked" was a convenience sample [^47].
OpenAI's configurations permit only Lean's three standard axioms (`propext`, `Quot.sound`, `Classical.choice`) and list no definition holes [^50].
Its own README warns that "many definition hole challenges can be gamed without additional oversight" [^13].
The Unique Games challenge, for example, defines its own encodings of 3SAT and translation games on top of Mathlib's polynomial-time Turing machine notion [^50,12].
The August 2026 human audit of OpenAI's earlier Astra results made the same point: "a formalization can encode the wrong proposition" [^40].
The zeta statement uses Mathlib's own `riemannZeta` and introduces no new definitions, so there is little room for a definitional trick [^51].
The overview lists, among others: "Proves Khot's Unique Games Conjecture" (102), "Proves L = RL = BPL" (103), and ω ≤ 9/4 over ℂ (107) [^15].
Number theory family 003 claims every Dirichlet L-function, ζ included, "is zero-free in Re s > 7/8", with a companion giving "a different proof of the zero-free half-plane Re s > 11/12" [^16,10].
No zero-free half-plane to the left of Re s = 1 has ever been established, which is why this family drew the most attention [^39].
OpenAI 107: all but finitely many characteristics
OpenAI's three bounds are from `lean/docs/107.md` [^11], and the prior record is from Alman et al. [^46].
Decades of incremental work moved ω by about 0.01. A drop to 2.25 would be the largest move since the 1980s.
Latent Space's AINews headline said the release solved "90 of the top 500 open math problems".
A KuCoin flash item claimed the Riemann Hypothesis itself had been proven [^45].
Startup Fortune said every result carried a machine-checkable proof [^49].
**What is genuinely new, independent of correctness:** (1) the scale, about 72 times the ten-result Astra release of 1 August [^48];
The Astra figures (ten results, all Lean-formalized) are from Kingy.ai's evidence review [^48] and the human audit [^40].
In October 2025 GPT-5's "solved" Erdős problems turned out to be literature lookups, which Thomas Bloom called "a dramatic misrepresentation" [^41].
Reports on two of the ten Astra results said they relied on uncited prior work [^48].

A spokesperson told Scientific American the model "produced almost every one of the results in response to a single prompt handed to a single AI agent", while conceding "some results might have taken multiple attempts" [^31].
The contrast with September's Navier–Stokes claim is large: that run used roughly 10,000 concurrent agents for about 88 hours [^42].
MIT's Andrew Sutherland put the methodological point bluntly: "treat any claims about one-shotting problems with a single agent as unverified … We should ask for receipts" [^31].

The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study, published guidelines on 29 September informed by more than 600 survey responses [^32].
Its members include Gowers, Hairer, Witten and Vakil [^32].
On release day it issued a statement that its involvement "should not be interpreted as a judgment of the impact of these results or an endorsement of the process" [^33].
OpenAI's spokesperson told Scientific American the company is "not bound by these recommendations" [^31].
The group's opening position was stronger still: "we ask them to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models" [^32].
Daniel Litt argued for openness: "I see no reason why we should ask the company to keep them secret from us" [^31].
Terence Tao, posting the same day, warned that "solutions to open problems are now being harvested at large scale in an unsustainable fashion" [^34].
Gil Kalai called it "an amazing milestone for mathematics" but added that "the results will needs to be verified and digested by human mathematicians in the months to come" [^35].
Thomas Bloom froze new proof claims on erdosproblems.com that day, and removed its solved counts, because most comments had become "people announcing AI-generated proofs" [^36].
AGMAI also called its talks with OpenAI "constructive" [^33].
